stem: A finance-ops agent has a tool that transfers funds between internal accounts. Leadership requires that this tool must never execute without a second human's explicit sign-off, with no exceptions, even if the request comes from an admin user or someone later edits the system prompt. An engineer proposes adding a bold instruction to the system prompt: "ALWAYS require human approval before calling transfer_funds."

options.text: The bold system-prompt instruction, since Claude reliably follows explicit capitalized directives
A one-time reminder appended to the first user message of each session
A deterministic approval gate in the tool-execution harness that blocks the transfer_funds call from completing until a second human explicitly confirms it
A note in the tool's description field stating that approval is required

explanation: "No exceptions" is a guarantee, and only code the harness enforces can provide one — text the model reads, no matter how it's phrased or where it's placed, remains a request the model could fail to follow, be argued out of, or simply misjudge. A deterministic gate in the harness can refuse to execute the transfer regardless of what the model outputs. The bold system-prompt line, a session reminder, and a tool-description note are all variations on the same failure: they place the control inside model-readable text rather than inside code that physically stops the call.
author: v1-new

stem: An internal chatbot lets employees query their own HR records through a tool that calls the HR database. Two employees in the same department report that when they ask nearly identical questions, one occasionally sees a fragment of the other's salary data mixed into the response. The engineering team wants to fix the root cause rather than add a warning banner to the chat.

options.text: Scope every HR-record query to the authenticated identity of the current user at the point the tool executes, rather than trusting the model to filter results in conversation
Add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude to only discuss the current user's own data
Fine-tune a smaller, cheaper model specifically for the HR chatbot
Log every conversation so leaks can be reviewed after the fact

explanation: Authorization has to be enforced where the query actually executes, scoped to the authenticated caller, not left to the model's judgment inside the conversation. A system-prompt instruction is advisory and can fail under model error or a crafted request, which is exactly the failure mode already occurring. Model size has no bearing on per-user data scoping. Logging is detective, not preventive; it documents leaks after they've already happened instead of stopping them.
author: v1-new

stem: A security engineer is auditing a Claude-powered agent's supply chain for integrity risk, even though the model itself has not been altered. The agent connects to three MCP servers pulled fresh from a public registry at every deployment with no version pinning, and its long-running memory file accumulates facts across sessions with no validation step before they're written.

options.text: Confidentiality failure, because MCP servers pulled from a public registry are inherently exposed
Memory integrity failure, because unvalidated facts can persist into every future session
Availability failure, because an MCP server might go offline during a deployment
Supply-chain integrity failure, because unpinned MCP servers can change behavior between deployments without review

explanation: The two integrity failure modes actually present are supply-chain integrity (unpinned dependencies pulled fresh each deploy can change agent behavior without any review step) and memory integrity (a persistent memory file that accepts new facts without validation lets a false fact compound forward into every later session). "Public registry" describes where the servers come from, not a confidentiality property of the data the agent handles, so that option mislabels the risk. Nothing in the scenario describes downtime, so availability doesn't apply here even though it's a real property in other contexts.
author: v1-new
